title: Understanding REST APIs with Postman
excerpt: APIs are everywhere, but understanding what happens behind a request is where things get interesting. This guide explores REST APIs through practical examples, covering requests, responses, authentication, testing, and troubleshooting.
html:
What is an API?

Imagine you are shopping on an e-commerce website.

You find a pair of headphones, add them to your cart, enter your delivery address, choose a payment method, and click Place Order.

What happens after you click that button?

The website doesn't simply save the order inside your browser. The frontend sends a request to the backend containing information such as the customer, products, quantity, price, address, and payment details.

The backend processes that request, stores or updates the necessary data, and sends a response back.

It might look something like this:

E-commerce Website
       |
       |  "Create this order"
       v
      API
       |
       |  Process request
       v
 Backend / Database
       |
       |  Order created
       v
      API
       |
       |  Response
       v
E-commerce Website

The API acts as the communication layer between different parts of the system.

For example, the frontend might send:

{"customerId": 101,"productId": 5001,"quantity": 2,"paymentMethod": "card"}

And the API might respond:

{"orderId": 78432,"status": "confirmed","message": "Order created successfully"}

The frontend doesn't need to know how the backend stores the order. It simply needs to know how to communicate with the API and how to understand its response.

This is why APIs are so useful when we need to test, investigate, or troubleshoot what is happening behind an application.

What Makes an API a REST API?

You will often hear the term REST API.

REST stands for Representational State Transfer. It isn't a programming language, framework, or tool. REST is an architectural style for designing systems that communicate over a network.

The easiest way to understand REST is to think in terms of resources.

In our e-commerce example, an order could be a resource:

/orders
/orders/78432

The first represents the collection of orders, while the second represents one particular order.

HTTP methods then describe what we want to do with that resource:

GET     /orders/78432
POST    /orders
PUT     /orders/78432
PATCH   /orders/78432
DELETE  /orders/78432

The URL tells us what we're working with, while the HTTP method tells us what we want to do.

That's the practical part of REST that you'll encounter most often.

REST also follows other principles, such as stateless communication, using standard HTTP semantics, and working with representations of resources, commonly JSON.

Are all APIs REST APIs?

No.

REST is only one approach to building APIs. You may also come across:

API Style

What you'll commonly see

REST

Resources, HTTP methods, commonly JSON

SOAP

XML-based messaging and formal contracts

GraphQL

Clients query for the exact data they need

gRPC

RPC-style communication, commonly using Protocol Buffers

For this article, we'll focus on REST because it gives us a practical way to understand HTTP requests, responses, investigation, and testing.

Our Practical API: Restful Booker

Instead of using imaginary examples for everything, let's work with a real public API.

We'll use Restful Booker, a simple hotel booking API designed for practicing API interactions.

Base URL:

https://restful-booker.herokuapp.com

API documentation:

https://restful-booker.herokuapp.com/apidoc/index.html

We'll use it to create bookings, retrieve them, update them, delete them, and then investigate what happens when things don't go as expected.

Setting Up Postman

Now that we have a basic idea of how an API works, we need a tool that lets us interact with one directly.

For this tutorial, we'll use Postman.

Postman is an API client that allows us to build HTTP requests, send them to an API, inspect the response, and add automated checks around that response.

After installing Postman, create a new HTTP Request.

At first, the interface may look like it has a lot going on. You don't need to understand everything immediately. The main areas we'll use are:

Method
URL
Params
Authorization
Headers
Body
Pre-request Script
Tests

Think of these as different parts of the conversation with the API.

Method tells the API what we want to do.

URL tells it where the request is going.

Params are used to pass query parameters.

Authorization is used when the API requires authentication.

Headers provide additional information about the request.

Body contains data we want to send to the server.

Pre-request Script lets us prepare data before sending the request.

Tests allow us to automatically verify the response.

We won't learn these as isolated Postman features. We'll introduce each one when we actually need it while working with Restful Booker.

GET: Let's Ask the API for Something

Let's start with a simple question:

"What bookings are available?"

In Postman, select:

GET

and enter:

https://restful-booker.herokuapp.com/booking

Click Send.

The API should return booking IDs similar to:

[{
    "bookingid": 1},{
    "bookingid": 2},{
    "bookingid": 3}]

We just made our first API request.

Notice that we didn't send a request body. We simply asked the server to return information.

Now suppose we want to see booking 1.

Change the URL to:

https://restful-booker.herokuapp.com/booking/1

Keep the method as GET and send it.

You should receive a response similar to:

{"firstname": "Jim","lastname": "Brown","totalprice": 111,"depositpaid": true,"bookingdates": {
    "checkin": "2018-01-01",
    "checkout": "2019-01-01"},"additionalneeds": "Breakfast"}

Now we can see an important REST pattern:

GET /booking

asks for the collection.

GET /booking/1

asks for one specific resource.

This distinction becomes useful when investigating API problems.

POST: Let's Create a Booking

GET was easy because we were only asking for data.

Now let's send some data to the server.

In Postman, select:

POST

and use:

https://restful-booker.herokuapp.com/booking

Go to:

Body → raw → JSON

and enter:

{"firstname": "John","lastname": "Doe","totalprice": 150,"depositpaid": true,"bookingdates": {
    "checkin": "2026-09-01",
    "checkout": "2026-09-05"},"additionalneeds": "Breakfast"}

Click Send.

The API should return a response containing a booking ID and the booking data.

For example:

{"bookingid": 123,"booking": {
    "firstname": "John",
    "lastname": "Doe",
    "totalprice": 150,
    "depositpaid": true,
    "bookingdates": {
      "checkin": "2026-09-01",
      "checkout": "2026-09-05"
    },
    "additionalneeds": "Breakfast"}}

The actual booking ID will be different when you run it.

This request introduces an important concept: the request body.

Request Body vs Response Body

The request body is what the client sends.

The response body is what the server sends back.

For our POST request, we sent:

{"firstname": "John","lastname": "Doe","totalprice": 150}

and received something similar to:

{"bookingid": 123,"booking": {
    "firstname": "John",
    "lastname": "Doe",
    "totalprice": 150}}

When investigating an API, comparing these two can tell you a lot.

Suppose you send:

{"totalprice": 150}

but the response contains:

{"totalprice": 0}

Now we have a useful investigation point.

Did the API receive 150 correctly? Did the backend process it incorrectly? Was the data transformed somewhere?

Instead of saying "the API isn't working", we now have something specific to investigate.

Headers: The Extra Information Around a Request

A request contains more than just a URL, method, and body.

It can also contain headers, which provide additional information to the server.

For JSON requests, you'll commonly see:

Content-Type: application/json

This tells the server:

"The request body I'm sending is JSON."

You may also see:

Accept: application/json

which tells the server that the client expects a JSON response.

Headers become even more important when authentication is involved.

For example, many APIs use:

Authorization: Bearer <token>

But before using a Bearer token just because we see the word "token", let's look at how Restful Booker actually handles authentication.

Authentication: Some Requests Need More Than a Body

So far, our GET and POST requests worked without authentication.

But Restful Booker's protected booking operations require authentication. This includes:

PUT /booking/{id}
PATCH /booking/{id}
DELETE /booking/{id}

Restful Booker supports authentication through its /auth endpoint. We can send our credentials there and receive a token.

The overall flow is:

POST /auth
     ↓
Username + Password
     ↓
Authentication Token
     ↓
Use Token
     ↓
PUT /booking/{id}
PATCH /booking/{id}
DELETE /booking/{id}

Let's do it step by step.

Getting an Authentication Token

Create a new request in Postman.

Select:

POST

and use:

https://restful-booker.herokuapp.com/auth

Go to:

Body → raw → JSON

and enter:

{"username": "admin","password": "password123"}

Make sure the request contains:

Content-Type: application/json

Then click Send.

A successful authentication request returns a token similar to:

{"token": "abc123"}

The actual token will be different when you run the request.

The idea is simple:

Username + Password
        ↓
       /auth
        ↓
 Authentication Token

We can now use that token when making protected booking requests.

A Small Note About Bearer Tokens

You will encounter Bearer tokens frequently when working with APIs.

A typical Bearer token request looks like:

Authorization: Bearer eyJhbGciOi...

The word Bearer tells the server that the value following it is an access token.

This pattern is commonly seen with APIs using OAuth 2.0, JWTs, and other token-based authentication mechanisms.

However, Restful Booker does not use the Bearer format for its protected booking requests.

Instead, the token obtained from /auth is sent using a cookie:

Cookie: token=abc123

This is a good example of why we shouldn't blindly assume how authentication works.

Two APIs can both use the word "token" but expect that token to be sent in completely different ways.

Always check the API documentation.

Using the Token With PUT

Now let's return to our booking.

Suppose the booking we created has ID 123.

We want to update it, so create:

PUT https://restful-booker.herokuapp.com/booking/123

This time, under Headers, add:

Content-Type: application/json
Cookie: token=abc123

Replace abc123 with the token returned from /auth.

Then use our booking body:

{"firstname": "David","lastname": "Smith","totalprice": 200,"depositpaid": false,"bookingdates": {
    "checkin": "2026-09-10",
    "checkout": "2026-09-15"},"additionalneeds": "Lunch"}

Send the request.

If the token is valid and the rest of the request is correct, the API can process the update.

Now follow it with:

GET /booking/123

and verify that the booking actually contains the updated values.

This gives us a more realistic testing flow:

Create
  ↓
Authenticate
  ↓
Update
  ↓
Retrieve
  ↓
Verify

PATCH: Change Only What You Need

Suppose the booking is correct except for the first name.

We don't necessarily want to send the entire booking again.

Use:

PATCH

with:

https://restful-booker.herokuapp.com/booking/123

and the same authentication cookie:

Cookie: token=abc123

For the body:

{"firstname": "Michael"}

After the PATCH request, send GET again.

Check that:

firstname  → changed
lastname   → unchanged
totalprice → unchanged

This is where PATCH becomes useful.

Method

Typical purpose

GET

Retrieve a resource

POST

Create a resource

PUT

Update/replace a resource representation

PATCH

Partially update a resource

DELETE

Delete a resource

DELETE: Remove the Booking

Now let's delete the booking.

Use:

DELETE

with:

https://restful-booker.herokuapp.com/booking/123

and:

Cookie: token=abc123

Send the request.

Then verify the result with:

GET /booking/123

The booking should no longer be available.

This gives us a complete CRUD-style flow:

POST
 ↓
GET
 ↓
PUT
 ↓
GET
 ↓
PATCH
 ↓
GET
 ↓
DELETE
 ↓
GET

We're not just checking individual endpoints anymore. We're checking how the API behaves as the resource moves through different states.

What Should We Look At in a Response?

Once you start sending requests, you'll notice that Postman gives you more than just JSON.

A response usually gives us:

Status Code
Response Body
Response Headers
Response Time

For example:

Status: 200 OK
Time: 180 ms

followed by the response body.

Each piece gives us different information.

The status code gives us the general outcome.

The response body tells us what data the server returned.

The headers provide additional metadata.

The response time can give us an early indication of a performance problem.

So when investigating an API, don't just look for a green 200.

Look at the complete response.

Common HTTP Status Codes

You don't need to memorize every HTTP status code. Start with the ones you'll encounter frequently.

Status Code

Meaning

Typical situation

200 OK

Request succeeded

Successful GET, PUT, PATCH

201 Created

Resource created

Successful POST

400 Bad Request

Request is invalid

Invalid body or parameters

401 Unauthorized

Authentication failed or missing

Invalid/missing credentials

403 Forbidden

Access is not allowed

Insufficient permission

404 Not Found

Resource doesn't exist

Invalid booking ID

500 Internal Server Error

Server-side failure

Unexpected backend error

These codes are clues, not the complete diagnosis.

A 404 isn't automatically a defect.

A 200 isn't automatically a successful test.

The expected behavior and actual response still need to be compared.

Now Let's Investigate an API Problem

Imagine someone tells you:

"The booking API is returning 404."

Don't immediately assume the API is broken.

Reproduce the request in Postman.

Suppose it is:

GET /booking/999999

and the API returns:

404 Not Found

First ask:

Does booking 999999 actually exist?

Send:

GET /booking

and check the returned IDs.

If 999999 isn't there, the 404 may be exactly what the API is supposed to return.

This is an important troubleshooting habit:

An error response isn't automatically a bug.

First understand what the API was asked to do and what the expected behavior should be.

Troubleshooting a 400 Bad Request

Now suppose our POST request returns:

400 Bad Request

Start by inspecting the request itself.

Check:

URL
HTTP method
Query parameters
Headers
Authentication
Request body
Required fields
Data types
JSON structure

For example, this is valid JSON:

{"firstname": "John","totalprice": 150}

But this isn't:

{"firstname": "John","totalprice": 150,}

The extra comma makes the JSON invalid.

A small request problem can result in a completely different response from the server.

This is why reproducing the request in Postman is often more useful than simply looking at an error message displayed by the frontend.

Troubleshooting 401 and 403

Authentication problems require a slightly different investigation.

If you receive:

401 Unauthorized

check:

Was authentication performed?
Was a token returned?
Is the token valid?
Was it sent correctly?
Are the credentials correct?

For Restful Booker specifically, remember that the protected booking requests use:

Cookie: token=<token>

not:

Authorization: Bearer <token>

If you receive:

403 Forbidden

the server may recognize the request but refuse to allow the operation.

The exact behavior depends on the API's authentication and authorization design, but the response gives you a useful direction for investigation.

When 200 OK Isn't Good Enough

Imagine we send:

PUT /booking/123

and receive:

200 OK

Looks good.

But when we send:

GET /booking/123

the old data is still there.

Now we have a problem.

The request succeeded at the HTTP level, but the actual system behavior isn't what we expected.

That's why an API test shouldn't simply be:

Request → 200 → Pass

A better approach is:

Request
   ↓
Status Code
   ↓
Response Body
   ↓
Expected Data
   ↓
Actual Data
   ↓
Pass / Fail

The status code is only one piece of evidence.

What If the API Is Slow?

Status codes aren't the only useful information.

Suppose:

GET /booking/123

returns:

200 OK

but takes 8 seconds.

The request technically succeeded, but something may still be wrong.

If the endpoint normally responds in a few hundred milliseconds, that sudden increase in response time is worth investigating.

Possible areas include:

Backend processing
Database queries
External service calls
Network problems
Server resource usage

Postman won't necessarily tell you the root cause, but it gives you useful evidence that the API is responding unusually slowly.

Turning Manual Checks Into Postman Tests

So far we've been checking responses manually.

That's fine while learning, but repetitive checks are exactly the kind of thing we can automate.

For example:

pm.test("Status code is 200", function () {
    pm.response.to.have.status(200);
});

We can also check whether a field exists:

pm.test("Response contains firstname", function () {
    const response = pm.response.json();

    pm.expect(response).to.have.property("firstname");
});

Or verify an actual value:

pm.test("Firstname is correct", function () {
    const response = pm.response.json();

    pm.expect(response.firstname).to.eql("John");
});

These are simple assertions, but they turn manual verification into repeatable checks.

Testing the Response After Creating a Booking

For our POST request, we can verify more than just the status code.

For example:

pm.test("Booking was created", function () {
    pm.response.to.have.status(200);
});

We can also check that the response contains a booking ID:

pm.test("Booking ID is returned", function () {
    const response = pm.response.json();

    pm.expect(response).to.have.property("bookingid");
});

And we can verify the booking data:

pm.test("Created booking has the expected firstname", function () {
    const response = pm.response.json();

    pm.expect(response.booking.firstname).to.eql("John");
});

The exact status code should always be based on the API's documented behavior rather than assuming every POST must return 201.

That's another useful API-testing habit:

Test against the API contract, not against assumptions.

Pre-request Scripts: Prepare Something Before Sending

Sometimes the request needs dynamic data.

Postman allows us to run JavaScript before sending a request using a Pre-request Script.

For example:

const randomNumber = Math.floor(Math.random() * 10000);

pm.environment.set("randomNumber", randomNumber);

We could then use that variable in our request:

{"firstname": "John","lastname": "User{{randomNumber}}","totalprice": 150,"depositpaid": true,"bookingdates": {
    "checkin": "2026-09-01",
    "checkout": "2026-09-05"}}

The basic flow is:

Pre-request Script
        ↓
Prepare data
        ↓
Send request
        ↓
Receive response
        ↓
Run tests

This becomes particularly useful when we don't want to hardcode the same values for every test.

Variables: Don't Hardcode Everything

Imagine having ten requests containing:

https://restful-booker.herokuapp.com

Changing the base URL later would mean editing every request.

Instead, create a variable:

baseUrl

with the value:

https://restful-booker.herokuapp.com

Then use:

{{baseUrl}}/booking

We can also store our booking ID:

{{bookingId}}

and authentication token:

{{token}}

A protected request could then look like:

PUT {{baseUrl}}/booking/{{bookingId}}

with:

Cookie: token={{token}}

This makes the collection easier to maintain and allows one request to pass information to another.

A Practical Authentication Flow With Variables

We can take this one step further.

After calling:

POST /auth

we receive:

{"token": "abc123"}

Instead of manually copying the token, we can capture it with a Postman test:

const response = pm.response.json();

pm.environment.set("token", response.token);

Now our protected requests can simply use:

Cookie: token={{token}}

This gives us a much cleaner flow:

POST /auth
    ↓
Receive token
    ↓
Store token
    ↓
PUT /booking/{{bookingId}}
    ↓
PATCH /booking/{{bookingId}}
    ↓
DELETE /booking/{{bookingId}}

This is where Postman starts becoming more than a tool for manually sending requests. We're building a reusable API workflow.

Putting Everything Together

Let's now look at the complete booking flow we've built:

POST /booking
      ↓
Create booking
      ↓
Store booking ID
      ↓
GET /booking/{id}
      ↓
Verify booking
      ↓
POST /auth
      ↓
Receive and store token
      ↓
PUT /booking/{id}
      ↓
GET /booking/{id}
      ↓
Verify full update
      ↓
PATCH /booking/{id}
      ↓
GET /booking/{id}
      ↓
Verify partial update
      ↓
DELETE /booking/{id}
      ↓
GET /booking/{id}
      ↓
Verify deletion

Each request now has a purpose.

We're creating data, retrieving it, authenticating when required, changing it, removing it, and verifying the resulting state.

API Testing vs API Investigation

There is a useful difference between testing an API and investigating an API issue.

During testing, we normally start with an expectation:

"If I send this request, I expect this response."

During investigation, we start with an unexpected result:

"I didn't expect this response. Why did I get it?"

The evidence we look at is largely the same:

Request
Headers
Authentication
Request Body
Status Code
Response Body
Response Headers
Response Time

The difference is what we're trying to find out.

Testing asks:

Does the API behave as expected?

Investigation asks:

Why isn't the API behaving as expected?

That's why knowing how to construct and inspect API requests is useful across development, testing, support, debugging, and integration work.

A Simple API Troubleshooting Mindset

When something goes wrong, don't jump straight to the backend.

Start with the request and work your way through the evidence:

Something went wrong
        ↓
Reproduce the request
        ↓
Check endpoint and method
        ↓
Check parameters
        ↓
Check headers
        ↓
Check authentication
        ↓
Check request body
        ↓
Check status code
        ↓
Check response body
        ↓
Compare expected vs actual
        ↓
Check response time
        ↓
Investigate backend/logs if necessary

Sometimes you'll find the problem immediately.

Maybe the wrong endpoint was used.

Maybe the authentication token wasn't sent.

Maybe a required field is missing.

Maybe the resource doesn't exist.

Maybe the API accepted the request but returned incorrect data.

And sometimes the request will look perfectly correct. That's when you may need to investigate server logs, databases, dependent services, or infrastructure.

The goal isn't to blindly follow a checklist.

The goal is to use the request and response as evidence.

Final Thoughts

APIs can seem complicated when you first encounter terms like REST, HTTP methods, headers, authentication, status codes, request bodies, and response bodies.

But once you follow an actual request from beginning to end, the picture becomes much simpler.

A client asks the API to do something.

The API processes the request.

The server returns a response.

With Postman, we can make that entire conversation visible.

We can create a booking with POST, retrieve it with GET, authenticate ourselves when required, update it with PUT, change part of it with PATCH, and remove it with DELETE.

Then we can go one step further.

We can inspect requests and responses, reproduce unexpected behavior, investigate status codes, verify authentication, compare expected and actual data, investigate response times, and turn our manual checks into repeatable Postman tests.

That's where API work becomes much more interesting.

The real value isn't simply knowing how to click Send in Postman.

It's being able to look at an API request and answer:

What did we send, what did the server do, what did it return, and does that behavior actually match what we expected?

Once you can answer those questions, Postman becomes much more than an API client. It becomes a practical tool for understanding, testing, investigating, and troubleshooting APIs.
author: Jahidur Rahman
